Title: Go Field Notebook
Summary: Build a tiny typed notebook CLI while learning modules, values, slices, maps, errors and table-driven tests.
Overview:
Build a room notebook that accepts small JSON records, validates names and coordinates, and prints a stable inventory. This is your first Go program, so the deliverable includes a working module, an error contract, tests and a short explanation of value versus reference behavior.

Your existing programming experience helps with loops and conditions. Go adds explicit types, multiple return values, zero values and a compiler that rejects unused imports. Practice these on a small artifact before colony grammar makes failures harder to isolate.

Deliverable

A CLI reading one JSON array from a file argument and printing one room per line in name order, plus table-driven tests for the pure validation function. This is a notebook format, not the lem-in format. Later projects reuse the Room record and error-handling pattern.
Refresher:
A module is the build unit named by go.mod; a package groups Go source files in a directory. package main plus func main() forms an executable. A capitalized identifier is exported. A zero-valued int is 0; a nil map can be read but must be initialized before assignment.

A slice is a view over an array. Copying its header does not deep-copy its elements. Map lookup returns a second boolean so a missing key can be distinguished from a stored zero. Functions commonly return (value, error); callers must decide what to do with a non-nil error.

type Point struct { X, Y int }
p := Point{X: -3, Y: 8}
points := []Point{p}
byName := make(map[string]Point)
byName["atrium"] = points[0]
q, exists := byName["exit"]
_, _ = q, exists // remove this teaching placeholder in real code

This example introduces types; it does not validate or sort notebook records. Use gofmt to format all Go files. Compile errors are useful feedback, not runtime error cases to recover from.
Spec:
Notebook contract

  1. Accept exactly one input path. Read a JSON array of objects with Name, X, Y. Use only the standard library. Reject malformed JSON, trailing JSON data, missing names and duplicate names.
  2. Names are nonempty ASCII letters, digits or underscore; the first character cannot be L or #. For this notebook, x/y are Go ints. Negative and coincident coordinates are valid.
  3. Print accepted rooms in ascending bytewise name order as name x y, one newline per record. Do not mutate the caller's slice when obtaining sorted output.
  4. Empty arrays are valid and print nothing. Validation errors produce no inventory and return a useful error identifying the offending record.
  5. Implement ValidateRooms and Inventory as pure functions. The supplied main only delegates to Run; implement JSON decoding and output wiring yourself.

Out of scope

No tunnels, terminal commands, pathfinding, persistent database or goroutines. This small input grammar is intentionally different from the later colony parser.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build -o notebook .
# Windows executable name: go build -o notebook.exe .
go run . testdata/rooms.json
Verification:
Concrete cases

The supplied JSON fixture contains z at (1,0) and a at (-2,5). After implementation, go run . testdata/rooms.json prints:

a -2 5
z 1 0
  • []: success and zero output bytes.
  • Two rooms named a: validation error and no inventory.
  • A room named Lbad or an empty name: validation error.
  • [, a missing file, and two consecutive JSON arrays: distinct error paths without panic.
  • A writer returning an error: Run propagates it.

Exit gate

Explain why map order cannot define output order, why zero coordinates are valid and why a returned error must be checked. Show gofmt-clean files and tests that verify output bytes and lack of caller mutation.

Title: Bounded File Reader
Summary: Build a CLI that reads physical lines safely, preserves accepted input and fails cleanly at size and I/O boundaries.
Overview:
Build a line inspection tool for colony files. Its job is to read a bounded file, normalize line endings under a stated policy and report numbered lines without interpreting rooms or links. You will isolate transport failures from semantic failures before introducing a grammar.

Reuse P01's module workflow, returned errors and output tests. The new material is io.Reader, file ownership, EOF, Scanner limits and a transactional output boundary. Deliver the reader package functions, a CLI, boundary fixtures and tests with injected readers and writers.
Refresher:
io.Reader.Read may return bytes and an error together. EOF is normal only after all returned bytes have been consumed. Small reads do not necessarily mean EOF. Use standard helpers instead of assuming one Read fills a buffer.

To distinguish exactly-at-limit from over-limit, request at most limit+1 bytes and reject if that extra byte exists. A bounded reader returning EOF at the limit cannot alone prove that the source ended there. Scanner token limits are a second, independent limit.

f, err := os.Open(path)
if err != nil { return err }
defer f.Close() // ownership begins after successful Open
// Pass f to your reader boundary; do not parse room names here.

Use injected readers for failure tests. A strings.Reader cannot simulate every filesystem failure, so a tiny custom Reader can return bytes followed by a sentinel error. Do not use goroutines merely because I/O is involved.
Spec:
Reader contract

  1. Implement ReadDocument(r, limits). Limits are positive; the academy default is 1 MiB total input and 4096 bytes per physical line, excluding CRLF/LF terminators.
  2. Accept LF and CRLF. Normalize CRLF to LF, reject any bare CR and NUL. Preserve every other byte, including comments, leading/trailing spaces and non-ASCII bytes; the next project decides grammar validity.
  3. A final newline is optional. Store logical lines without terminators and an echo string containing the normalized lines joined by LF with exactly one final LF. An empty file returns an empty document; P03 rejects it as a colony.
  4. Do not invent an empty final line from a final newline. Preserve an actual interior blank line for the parser to reject later. Both byte and line limits apply before further allocation grows beyond the bound.
  5. The CLI requires one file path and prints numbered lines in the form 1: text. Reader, size, usage and writer failures return errors; no partial report is printed before the complete read succeeds.
  6. Do not close a caller-owned Reader. Run owns the file it opens. Check Scanner.Err if using Scanner; configure its buffer from the line policy.

No colony validation or pathfinding belongs in this tool. The normalized Echo is a deliberate academy policy; upstream only asks for accepted content to be displayed.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build -o line-reader .
# Windows executable name: go build -o line-reader.exe .
go run . testdata/lines.txt
Verification:
Known cases

The fixture has the lines 3, # note and ##start. The report must be:

1: 3
2: # note
3: ##start
  • With MaxBytes=4, abcd succeeds; abcde fails without output.
  • With MaxLine=3, abc plus LF succeeds; abcd plus LF fails.
  • LF and CRLF inputs compare equal after normalization. A bare CR or NUL fails.
  • Input a followed by two LF characters contains one actual blank line; input a followed by one LF does not gain one.
  • Reader failure after a prefix and writer failure during final output are propagated.

Exit gate

Show exact byte counts at both limits. Explain why a successful read is not a valid colony and why a partial read must not be echoed as accepted input.

Title: Colony Grammar State Machine
Summary: Build a line-oriented parser with explicit phases, pending terminal markers, source locations and adversarial grammar tests.
Overview:
Build a colony inspection CLI that accepts a bounded text document and returns a validated colony model. It stops before graph search. The useful artifact is a parser whose errors identify the physical line and whose accepted document can later be echoed without reconstruction.

Reuse P02's reader and normalized Echo contract. Replace P01's notebook grammar with the actual lem-in language. Keep parsing and graph traversal separate: an otherwise valid disconnected colony can parse successfully, then fail reachability in P05.
Refresher:
A parser state records what is legal next. This grammar needs ants → rooms → links, a pending terminal marker, the room dictionary and a canonical edge set. A pending marker is not a boolean start/end room: it must attach to the next room across comments and unknown commands.

type Phase uint8
const (
    ExpectAnts Phase = iota
    ReadRooms
    ReadLinks
)
type Location struct { Line int } // physical line, starting at 1

Recognition order matters. Classify comments and exact commands before trying room or tunnel syntax. Numeric conversion must inspect its error. For hyphenated names, a blind Split on '-' loses information: examine all hyphen positions against the complete room dictionary and require one valid endpoint pair.

Read the hub's academy contract before coding. It is part of this project's spec, including choices that upstream leaves ambiguous.
Spec:
Accepted language

  1. Implement Parse(lines) with phases ants, rooms, links. Preserve source line numbers. Leading/trailing horizontal whitespace may surround a data line; it remains present in Echo. Interior blank lines are invalid. Comments begin with # after trimming; exact ##start and ##end are recognized commands, other ## lines are ignored semantically.
  2. The first data line is [1-9][0-9]*, in range 1..10000. This no-sign/no-leading-zero rule is academy policy. Commands before the count may be ignored only if unknown; recognized terminal commands there are invalid.
  3. A room has exactly three whitespace-separated fields: name, x, y. The name is valid UTF-8, nonempty, contains no Unicode whitespace or controls, and begins with neither L nor #. Hyphens are allowed. Coordinates match optional sign plus decimal digits and fit a signed 64-bit Go int; use a 64-bit target. Coincident coordinates and unordered names are valid.
  4. Exactly one distinct start and one distinct end must be defined. A marker applies to the next room, skipping comments and unknown commands. Another terminal marker while one is pending, a repeated marker, a marker after links or EOF while pending is invalid.
  5. Room names cannot repeat. At the first tunnel, freeze room definitions. A tunnel has no whitespace and must have exactly one split at a hyphen whose left and right strings are known room names. Zero matches or multiple matches are invalid. Reject self-links and duplicate undirected pairs, including reversed duplicates.
  6. Reject a room after links, unknown noncommand lines, bad arity, invalid integers, overflow and missing terminals. Unknown commands are ignored even after the links start. Ordinary cycles and isolated extra rooms are permitted at this stage.
  7. Return no partial Colony on error. Store rooms by insertion order and terminals by integer index. P04 will canonicalize adjacency; Parse does not decide routes or turn count.

Limits and CLI

Apply P02's limits, plus at most 10000 rooms and 50000 links. The inspection CLI prints ants=N rooms=R links=E start=NAME end=NAME after full validation. An invalid-data error begins ERROR: invalid data format; this prep program may return it to main on stderr. L01 adopts the final stdout error policy.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/colony.txt
Verification:
Fixture

The supplied colony must inspect as ants=3 rooms=3 links=2 start=s end=t. Parsing is not yet proof of reachability.

Mutation table

  • Replace 3 by 0, -1, 01 or an overflowing integer: invalid count.
  • Delete ##end, repeat ##start, or leave ##end pending at EOF: invalid terminal definition.
  • Add s with different coordinates: duplicate name. Give s and m equal coordinates: accepted.
  • Add m-s when s-m exists: duplicate undirected link. Add m-m: self-link. Add m-ghost: unknown endpoint.
  • Add an ordinary cycle among distinct rooms: accepted. Add a blank data line or room after links: rejected.
  • Insert an unknown command between ##start and s: accepted and start remains s.
  • Exercise the unique and ambiguous hyphen cases from the tunnel chapter.

Exit gate

Every invalid case returns an error with the required prefix and a useful physical line, no panic and no usable partial model. Keep echo bytes from P02; never rebuild them from parsed records.

Title: Undirected Graph Inventory
Summary: Build a stable adjacency-list graph and an inventory of components, degrees and cycles without enumerating all routes.
Overview:
Build an inspection tool that turns validated room and tunnel records into a graph. It reports stable adjacency, connected components and whether an undirected cycle exists. The graph representation becomes a shared boundary for BFS, simulation and planning.

Reuse P03's identity rules and canonical undirected edge pairs. Add integer vertex IDs, sorted adjacency and iterative graph traversal. You do not need flow theory yet. A disconnected extra room is useful information; it is not automatically a malformed colony.
Refresher:
A graph has vertices (rooms) and edges (tunnels). An adjacency list stores only actual neighbors, using O(V+E) space for an undirected graph where each edge appears twice. A dense V×V table is unnecessary for sparse colonies.

Names belong at the boundary. Give each room a stable integer index; use that index in arrays for visited flags and parents. For reproducibility across input reorderings, assign IDs after sorting names bytewise, then sort each neighbor list.

type Graph struct {
    Names []string
    Adj [][]int
}
// A room's coordinate is display metadata, not an edge weight.

In an undirected DFS, the edge back to the parent is not a cycle by itself. Detect a visited neighbor that is not the parent. Use an explicit stack to avoid recursion depth depending on hostile file structure. Never enumerate all simple paths merely to find connected components.
Spec:
1. Build an immutable Graph from unique names and canonical links. Revalidate indices and duplicate/self-edge invariants at this public boundary even if P03 normally guarantees them.
  2. Assign integer IDs by sorted names. Store every undirected tunnel exactly once in each endpoint's adjacency list; sort neighbors by the stable IDs.
  3. Report every connected component with names sorted inside it, and components ordered by their smallest name. Include isolated rooms.
  4. Report each vertex's degree and whether any ordinary cycle occurs. A triangle is valid and cyclic. A two-vertex single edge is acyclic.
  5. Do not use coordinates as distances, compare room names numerically or assume input order is a topological order.
  6. Use iterative traversals with O(V+E) work after canonical sorting. Copy mutable input slices if callers might retain them.
  7. The CLI accepts a small JSON graph fixture, prints adjacency lines a: b c, then components=N cyclic=true|false. No pathfinding or ant scheduling yet.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/graph.json
Verification:
The fixture has a triangle a-b-c-a and isolated z. Expected adjacency is a: b c; b: a c; c: a b; z: followed by no neighbors, then components=2 cyclic=true.

  • A single a-b edge: two degrees of 1, one component, no cycle.
  • A triangle: all degrees 2, one component, cycle true.
  • Triangle plus z: two components; cyclic remains true.
  • Duplicate reversed edge, self-edge or unknown name: error.
  • Permute all names and links repeatedly: exact inventory bytes remain equal.

Exit gate

Explain the two adjacency entries per tunnel, prove each vertex is visited at most once and show why coordinates play no role. Document sorting cost separately from linear traversal cost.

Title: Queue and BFS Route Finder
Summary: Build a queue, shortest-distance search and parent-based route reconstruction that handles cycles and unreachable destinations.
Overview:
Build a shortest-route inspector for an unweighted colony graph. It prints the shortest distance and one deterministic route, or a clear unreachable result. This is the correct tool for one ant's minimum travel time and a lower bound for many ants.

Reuse P04's canonical graph. You will build a queue with a head index, discover vertices once and reconstruct a path from parents. The artifact deliberately stops before claiming that one shortest route is an optimal multi-ant plan.
Refresher:
BFS explores all vertices at distance k before distance k+1. Each tunnel costs one turn for one ant, regardless of coordinate length. Set a vertex's parent and distance when it is discovered, then enqueue it once.

queue := make([]int, 0, len(g.Adj))
head := 0
// Your search owns discovery and enqueueing.
// Advancing head avoids repeatedly removing index zero.

Use a sentinel such as -1 for undiscovered distance or a separate seen slice. A parent value of 0 cannot by itself mean undiscovered because vertex 0 is real. Path reconstruction walks destination → parent → source and then reverses that list. An unreachable destination has no parent chain to follow.

BFS gives an O(V+E) search with an O(V) queue and metadata. Enumerating all simple paths is potentially exponential and is unnecessary for this task.
Spec:
1. Implement Shortest(g,start,end) returning one path including both endpoints and its edge count. Validate indices and adjacency integrity.
  2. Use P04's sorted neighbors so equal-length route selection is deterministic. Mark discovery before enqueueing.
  3. For start==end return a one-vertex path and distance 0 in this general-purpose tool. The final colony grammar requires distinct terminals.
  4. For an unreachable target return a distinguishable error and no path. Ordinary cycles and disconnected extra rooms must not cause nontermination.
  5. Path length in edges equals len(path)-1; every consecutive pair must be adjacent. Bound reconstruction to V parent steps to detect a broken invariant.
  6. The CLI's JSON has Names, Links, Start and End. Print distance=D path=name,name,.... Coordinates do not affect route choice.
  7. Include queue tests and a justification of shortestness using distance layers. This tool does not allocate multiple ants or promise minimum completion turns for them.

go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/routes.json
Verification:
The fixture contains the two-edge route s-a-t and the three-edge route s-b-c-t. Expect distance=2 path=s,a,t.

  • Direct s-t: distance 1 and path [s,t].
  • Diamond with equal routes: stable choice through lexically earlier neighbor a.
  • Disconnected t: unreachable error and no route.
  • Triangle on the way to t: terminate with the shortest route, never loop.
  • General-purpose start==end: distance 0 and one endpoint.
  • For every returned route, independently check all edges and len(path)-1.

Exit gate

Explain shortestness by BFS layers, show at most one discovery per vertex and state why this is only a lower bound for multiple ants.

Title: Turn Safety Simulator
Summary: Build an independent batch movement validator for room occupancy, undirected tunnel use, ant identity and completion.
Overview:
Build a replay checker that accepts a graph, initial ant positions and proposed movement turns. It must decide whether each turn is legal and advance state only after a complete valid batch. The checker will later challenge the planner without importing planner logic.

Reuse P04's graph and P05's reachability vocabulary. Logical concurrency here means that multiple ants move during one turn; goroutines are unnecessary. The artifact is a deterministic state transition function with adversarial tests, not a route planner.
Refresher:
A turn is a batch of intents derived from the previous state. First check each ant and edge, then account for all departures and arrivals. Final occupancy of an ordinary room cannot exceed one. Start/end have unlimited occupancy; their tunnels still have capacity one.

For s-a-b-t with ants at a and b, a turn moving b→t and a→b is legal. Validate the batch independently of token order. Two opposite moves a→b and b→a use the same undirected tunnel twice and are illegal, even though final occupancy looks harmless.

type Move struct { Ant, To int } // Ant is 1-based, To is a room ID
// Derive each source from the previous positions, never from an untrusted token.

Copy state before applying a successful turn or construct next positions separately. A rejected turn must leave previous positions byte-for-byte unchanged. Finished ants remain at end. Waiting is absence from the movement list.
Spec:
1. Implement Step(g,start,end,positions,moves), where positions[i] is ant i+1's room. Validate the initial positions and all room IDs.
  2. For each intent, require ant in 1..n, at most one intent for that ant, an existing undirected tunnel and a different destination. An ant already at end cannot leave.
  3. Use a canonical unordered endpoint pair to ensure each tunnel is used at most once across both directions during the turn.
  4. Compute all departures and arrivals from the old state. A room vacated this turn may receive one ant. Reject two arrivals to the same ordinary room or an arrival into a stationary occupied room.
  5. Start and end permit multiple ants. Waiting is legal, but no empty movement turn is accepted in a completed canonical solution stream. The general Step API can validate an empty batch as unchanged state.
  6. Do not mutate positions or moves on either success or failure. Return next positions only after the entire batch passes.
  7. The CLI reads a JSON replay with a graph and turns, starts all ants at start, prints valid turns=T arrived=N only if all ants reach end. An incomplete replay is a distinct error.

The academy uses simultaneous turns with departures before arrivals. Cyclic rotations around three or more rooms are batch-valid under this convention; L01 can normalize closed per-turn movement cycles to waits before output. This choice is explicit because upstream does not fully define within-turn ordering.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/replay.json
Verification:
The two-ant s-a-t fixture has three turns and must print valid turns=3 arrived=2.

  • Reverse tokens in the middle turn: still valid.
  • Send two ants into a during the first turn: room and tunnel violations.
  • Move ant1 twice in one turn: reject before state changes.
  • Move into an occupied room whose occupant waits: reject.
  • Swap two ants on one edge: reject shared tunnel usage.
  • Let two distinct terminal-adjacent edges deliver to end in one turn: accepted.
  • End the stream after turn 2: incomplete. Let a finished ant leave end: rejected.

Exit gate

Demonstrate atomic rejection, order-independent batch validation and final all-ant completion. Do not use this checker to infer optimality; a slow schedule can be perfectly legal.

Title: Traffic and Ant Allocation Lab
Summary: Build a deadline calculator for known disjoint routes and expose why permanently reserving the first shortest path can lose.
Overview:
Build an allocation calculator for a supplied set of internally vertex-disjoint start-to-end paths. It finds the smallest completion deadline supported by those paths and constructs a valid pipeline. Then compare two supplied route sets on a colony where a greedy shortest-path reservation performs worse.

Reuse P05's distance vocabulary and P06's movement checker. This project teaches throughput, makespan and allocation without pretending that its restricted route-set calculator solves the whole colony problem. The counterexample motivates residual rerouting in P08.
Refresher:
Makespan is the number of turns until the last ant arrives. For a path of length l edges used as a pipeline, its first ant arrives at turn l and each further ant can arrive one turn later. By deadline T it can deliver max(0,T-l+1) ants. This formula also gives T deliveries for a direct edge, respecting one use of that edge per turn.

For internally disjoint paths, sum those capacities. A deadline can carry n ants exactly when the sum is at least n. Allocate no more than each path's capacity and stop once n ants are assigned. The formula applies to the supplied independent paths; overlapping paths share rooms or edges and invalidate the simple sum.

Compare lengths [2,4] for four ants: T=3 carries 2+0, T=4 carries 3+1. Sending all four down the shortest path takes five turns. Good allocation can improve a fixed route set, but finding that set is a different problem.
Spec:
1. Implement Allocate(lengths,n) for positive path lengths and positive n. Return the minimum feasible integer deadline and counts per path, with sum counts=n.
  2. Preserve input path order for equal decisions. At the minimum deadline, allocate up to each path's deadline capacity in supplied order until all ants are assigned. Zero allocation is permitted.
  3. Use checked arithmetic and early capacity saturation at n; reject negative/zero lengths, nonpositive n and representational overflow.
  4. Build a schedule generator for explicitly supplied internally vertex-disjoint paths. Assign ant IDs by path order then launch order; advance existing ants before launching the next ant on each path. Check the result with P06.
  5. Reject overlapping ordinary rooms, duplicate path edges and malformed paths at the schedule boundary. Unlimited start/end do not authorize a duplicated direct tunnel.
  6. The CLI fixture uses lengths [2,4], n=4; print turns=4 counts=3,1.
  7. Submit a written counterexample: edges s-a, a-b, b-t, a-c, c-d, d-t, s-e, e-f, f-b. Reserving shortest s-a-b-t permanently blocks two disjoint routes s-a-c-d-t and s-e-f-b-t. For four ants, compare the shortest-only six-turn pipeline with the two-route five-turn pipeline. This demonstrates greedy failure; prove global optimality later with P11.

go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/allocation.json
Verification:
• Lengths [2,4], n=4: turns=4, counts=[3,1].
  • Lengths [1], n=3: turns=3, counts=[3]; never three ants through the direct tunnel at once.
  • Lengths [3,3], n=4: turns=4, counts=[2,2].
  • Length zero, n zero and empty route list: error.
  • A supplied overlapping path pair: reject before using the additive capacity formula.
  • The greedy counterexample: demonstrate a legal five-turn alternative to the six-turn shortest-only plan.

For each result, show feasibility at T and infeasibility at T-1 within the fixed route set. Explicitly state that this calculator is not a general minimum-turn colony solver.

Title: Residual Flow Workbench
Summary: Build an integral max-flow engine with reverse arcs, augmenting BFS, flow conservation and cut witnesses.
Overview:
Build a directed network workbench that sends integral flow from a source to a sink. It reports the achieved value, per-original-edge flow and a reachable-side cut after exhaustion. Reverse arcs let the algorithm cancel part of an earlier decision, addressing the greedy failure exposed in P07.

Reuse the BFS worklist pattern from P05, but search only arcs with positive residual capacity. No rooms or time layers are hidden inside this engine. Keeping the engine generic lets P09 test the modelling reduction separately.
Refresher:
For an original arc u→v with capacity c and flow f, forward residual capacity is c-f and reverse residual capacity is f. Traversing a reverse arc cancels earlier flow; it does not represent an ant walking backward in the final colony.

Store a reverse index on every residual arc. Adding an original arc creates a forward residual arc and a paired zero-capacity reverse arc. If both u→v and v→u exist as original arcs, each gets its own pair; do not accidentally merge independent original capacities.

An augmenting path carries its smallest residual capacity, the bottleneck. Update both directions of every pair. At every nonterminal vertex, incoming original flow equals outgoing original flow. Integral starting capacities and integral bottlenecks preserve integral flows.

When no residual path reaches the sink, the source-reachable vertices form a cut whose original outgoing capacity equals the achieved flow. That certifies maximum flow. A target-capped run that stops early proves target feasibility but does not automatically yield a minimum cut.
Spec:
1. Implement a mutable Network with stable original-edge handles, adjacency lists and paired reverse indices. Reject negative capacities, invalid endpoints and source==sink. Zero capacity is allowed.
  2. Use BFS to find augmenting paths through positive residual arcs. Store parent arc identities, not merely parent vertices, because multiple arcs can share endpoints.
  3. Find a bottleneck, update forward and reverse residual capacities and repeat until no path or a supplied nonnegative target value is reached. Never augment beyond the remaining target.
  4. Return the achieved flow and permit extraction of original-edge flows. Repeated calls on the same residual state must have an explicitly documented meaning; this academy API resets from original capacities for each Solve call.
  5. Verify bounds 0≤f≤c and conservation. On exhausted runs, report a source-reachable cut and compare its capacity with value. Do not claim cut equality on an early target stop.
  6. Use integer capacities and checked additions. This engine uses O(V+E) storage. BFS augmentation has general O(VE²) worst-case cost; with target n and integral capacities, no more than n successful augmentations are needed, giving O(n(V+E)) for the capped task.
  7. The CLI JSON provides V, Arcs, Source, Sink and Target. The fixture's target is 2 and it prints flow=2. No room splitting or timetable logic yet.
Run:

go vet ./...
go run . testdata/network.json
Verification:
• Unit diamond s-a-t and s-b-t: target 2 achieves 2.
  • Capacity 2 into a followed by capacity 1 out: max flow 1 and exhausted cut 1.
  • No source-sink path: flow 0 without error; this is a feasible network with no throughput.
  • Forced initial s-a-b-t augmentation: residual cancellation permits value 2.
  • Antiparallel original arcs preserve separate identities and nonnegative residuals.
  • Target 1 on a capacity-2 network stops at 1 and makes no unjustified maximum-cut claim.
  • Negative capacity, invalid endpoints and integer overflow are rejected.

Title: Capacity Through Time
Summary: Build a time-expanded network that models room occupancy, waiting and one shared use of every undirected tunnel per turn.
Overview:
Build a model compiler: given a colony graph, an ant count and a deadline T, emit a directed capacity network for P08. The network answers whether all ants can reach end by T. The deliverable includes metadata linking network arcs back to rooms and turns, a printed small-network inventory and a written correspondence argument.

Reuse P06's batch semantics and P08's integral flow engine. The new concepts are vertex splitting, time layers, holdovers and a shared tunnel gadget. This modelling project is separate from searching for the best deadline, which comes in P10.
Refresher:
A static max-flow graph measures throughput, not a completion deadline. Time expansion gives each room a copy at every boundary k=0..T. A unit flow travels from start at time 0 to end at time T.

Split each room-time copy into in and out nodes. The in→out arc has capacity 1 for an ordinary room and n for start/end. A holdover out(v,k)→in(v,k+1) represents waiting and uses the same boundary occupancy limits.

For each physical tunnel {u,v} and turn k→k+1, create two gadget nodes ein/eout with one capacity-1 bottleneck ein→eout. Connect out(u,k) and out(v,k) into ein; connect eout to in(u,k+1) and in(v,k+1). All gadget connector capacities are 1. Both directions share the bottleneck, so an opposing swap cannot consume the tunnel twice.

The gadget also permits entering and leaving on the same side. Interpret that as waiting, not a self-tunnel move, and normalize it to the holdover during extraction. It cannot create extra movement capacity. Do not add gadget entry connectors from end: end is absorbing, while its holdovers retain arrivals through T.
Spec:
Network contract

  1. Implement Expand for a validated undirected graph, distinct terminals, positive n and nonnegative T. Return nodes, original arcs, source/sink IDs and arc metadata.
  2. Create two nodes for every (room,k), k=0..T, with capacity 1 or n as described. Use source=in(start,0) and sink=out(end,T); cap total requested flow at n.
  3. Create holdovers for every room across adjacent time layers, capacity 1 for ordinary rooms and n at terminals. An ant that arrives early stays at end; no real movement leaves end.
  4. Create one shared capacity-1 gadget per undirected tunnel per time step. Omit endpoint-entry connectors from end. Endpoint output connectors may lead to end or back to the same endpoint. Preserve physical tunnel identity and time in metadata.
  5. Never model an undirected tunnel as two independent capacity-1 movement arcs: that would allow a forbidden opposing swap. Never use n as a direct start-end tunnel's capacity.
  6. Node IDs and original arc insertion order are deterministic from P04's canonical room and edge ordering. Metadata distinguishes room, wait, connector and bottleneck arcs without trying to infer meaning from numeric IDs later.
  7. Before allocation, calculate checked upper counts: Vt=2(T+1)V+2TE and Et≤(2T+1)V+5TE original arcs. Residual storage doubles Et. Reject a configured budget breach as resource exhaustion, not malformed colony or infeasible deadline.

Correspondence argument

A legal schedule gives integral flow by following room splits, waits and each moved tunnel gadget; continue early arrivals through end holdovers. Capacities follow from batch room occupancy and shared tunnel use. Conversely, integral value-n flow decomposes into n source-sink walks in the original time DAG. Read each layer transition as a move or wait; normalize same-side gadget uses into waits. Room splits and bottlenecks then enforce all P06 constraints. No flow means fewer than n ants can meet that deadline. Absorbing end is without loss: keeping an arrived ant there frees rather than consumes nonterminal resources.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/deadline.json
Verification:
• s-a-t, n=2: T=2 max flow 1; T=3 max flow 2.
  • Direct s-t, n=3: T=2 max flow 2; T=3 max flow 3.
  • Two length-two disjoint branches, n=2: T=2 max flow 2, with both arriving at end together.
  • A stationary occupied ordinary room blocks another arrival even if incoming tunnels differ.
  • Both directional uses of one tunnel-time share the bottleneck.
  • A same-side gadget traversal is extracted as a wait and never printed as a self move.
  • Counts just above a configured network budget produce a resource error before allocation; this is not deadline infeasibility.

Exit gate

Provide an annotated tiny network, the two-way correctness argument and countertests that fail if room splitting or the shared bottleneck is removed.

Title: Exact Deadline Planner
Summary: Build a minimum-turn planner from deadline feasibility, integral trajectory extraction and deterministic ant identities.
Overview:
Build a planner library that takes an already validated graph and returns a minimum-turn schedule. It combines P05's distance lower bound, P09's deadline model and P08's integral max flow. It also extracts concrete ant trajectories and validates their movements with P06.

This is the last isolated algorithm build before integration. Do not add colony parsing here. The deliverable includes a schedule, a neighboring-deadline infeasibility witness and a correctness argument covering the search, reduction and extraction rather than only the flow engine.
Refresher:
Let d be the BFS distance from start to end. No ant can arrive before d. Routing all n ants through one shortest simple path as a pipeline finishes by d+n-1, so that is a proven finite upper bound, including d=1.

Define F(T) as whether deadline T supports value n in the time-expanded network. F is monotone: extend a feasible schedule by keeping every finished ant at end. Binary search finds the first feasible T in [d,d+n-1]; a linear scan is also exact but uses more probes. A resource error is a third result, separate from true and false.

After the successful flow is found, decompose its positive original flow into n unit source-sink trajectories. The original network is a DAG ordered by time and gadget stage, so repeated unit extraction terminates. Ignore reverse residual arcs. Translate split/connector metadata into one room per boundary, normalize same-side gadget use to waiting and keep early arrivals at end.

Give trajectories ant IDs 1..n in deterministic extraction order. At each turn emit only IDs whose room changed, in increasing ID order. The planner assigns ants to time trajectories directly; P07's route-length allocation is a useful special case, not an extra heuristic step.
Spec:
1. Implement Plan for canonical graph data. Preflight BFS: no route returns a no-route error. Ordinary cycles and irrelevant disconnected components remain valid.
  2. Use checked d+n-1, then binary search the first feasible deadline using fresh P09/P08 state for each probe. A budget or cancellation error aborts with that distinct error; never treat it as infeasibility or fall back to a greedy answer labelled optimal.
  3. Rebuild or retain a successful model at the final T and extract exactly n integral trajectories. Validate every forward-flow unit, complete source-sink traversal and one room assignment per ant per boundary.
  4. Use stable room/edge/model ordering and always choose the first available original outgoing arc in that order for unit extraction. Ant IDs follow extraction order. Do not use map iteration or timing to break ties.
  5. Convert trajectories to moves, omit waits and sort tokens by ant ID. End is absorbing. Under the academy batch policy, a closed rotation is legal but unnecessary; it may be retained, or normalized only with a documented identity-preserving transformation and tests.
  6. Check every turn with P06 and require all ants at end. A positive empty turn in a minimum schedule would permit removing that idle turn; detect it as an invariant failure rather than printing a blank movement line.
  7. For T>d, retain an exhausted max-flow result for T-1 showing value<n and a cut with that value. For T=d, BFS provides the lower bound. Explain why feasibility at T and infeasibility at T-1 prove global minimum turns.
  8. Let U=d+n-1. With capped BFS flow and O(T(V+E)) model size, one probe costs O(nT(V+E)) and O(T(V+E)) memory. O(log n) probes give O(nU(V+E)log(n+1)) as a safe high-level bound, plus extraction/output. Storing all trajectories adds O(nT) integer cells; preflight the academy ant-time-cell budget or use a proven bounded sparse representation. Bound storage and work before allocation and include emitted token cost.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/planner.json
Verification:
• s-a-t, n=3: minimum 4 turns; T=3 flow<3.
  • Direct s-t, n=3: minimum 3; one tunnel use each turn.
  • Two disjoint length-two branches, n=3: minimum 3; T=2 carries only two.
  • P07 greedy counterexample, n=4: a five-turn plan beats shortest-only six; P11 will independently confirm minimum five.
  • Unreachable end: no-route error. Add an isolated irrelevant room to a valid graph: same optimum.
  • Same input 20 times: identical ant IDs, turn count and token order.
  • Inject a model-budget failure: distinct resource error, no claimed optimal schedule.

Exit gate

Submit the schedule, P06 replay result and the T-1 cut or BFS distance witness. Explain bounds, monotonicity, integrality, reduction correctness and extraction. A greedy route-set selection cannot replace any of these arguments.

Title: Adversarial Validator and Tiny Oracle
Summary: Build a transcript checker, hostile fixture suite and exhaustive occupancy-state oracle that independently tests minimum-turn claims.
Overview:
Build two review tools: a black-box checker for a complete lem-in transcript and a tiny exhaustive optimality oracle. The checker proves legality and completion; the oracle explores joint occupancy states instead of using flow, providing independent evidence about minimum turns on small colonies.

Reuse P03's declared grammar, P06's move invariants and P10's planner as a system under test. Keep the oracle independent from the time-expanded model and residual engine. The delivered artifact includes reproducible random seeds, named adversarial fixtures, mutation tests and a discrepancy report.
Refresher:
A transcript contains a normalized accepted-input echo, one empty separator line, then movement lines. Tokens encode only ant ID and destination, so derive each source from replay state. Split after the first hyphen following the ant number; the destination itself may contain hyphens.

A small oracle can search the finite set of occupancy states. A state is a sorted multiset of room IDs occupied by n indistinguishable ants; repeated IDs are legal only at start/end. For each state, enumerate each ant's wait or adjacent move choices, reject shared tunnel use and invalid next occupancy, sort the next multiset and perform BFS over states. Keep end absorbing. This is a different algorithm from flow.

State BFS depth is the number of turns. The first all-end state proves minimum turns because every legal next batch was considered. Keep the tiny limit explicit: V≤6 and n≤3 for the academy oracle, plus state/transition budgets. Exceeding a budget means unknown, not no route.
Spec:
1. Implement a bounded transcript checker requiring the full echo and exactly one blank separator. Reparse the echoed colony under the published policy, then validate movement spelling, ant IDs, known destination names, no duplicate IDs per line and ID-ascending canonical output.
  2. Apply P06 batch rules to every movement line. Reject empty movement lines, extra diagnostics, unfinished ants, movement after completion and invalid EOF. Require the accepted echo to match the submitted input after P02 normalization when the original file is supplied.
  3. Implement Oracle with exhaustive occupancy-state BFS, not P08/P09 calls. Return the first all-end depth or no-route only after complete bounded exhaustion. A budget breach is a distinct error.
  4. Enumerate wait/move combinations from each old state, enforce undirected edge use and boundary room occupancy independently, then canonicalize indistinguishable ants. End ants only wait. Preserve reproducible parent metadata for a discrepancy witness.
  5. Cross-check planner turns against oracle turns over every simple labelled graph with V=2..5, fixed terminals 0 and V-1 and n=1..3, within the chosen budgets. Include disconnected graphs. Add fixed-seed random V=6 cases and preserve exact seeds if you run them.
  6. Include direct edge, single corridor, diamond, bottleneck, cycles, disconnected extras, no route, hyphenated names and P07's greedy trap. Mutate accepted transcripts to target every checker rejection rule.
  7. The CLI fixture uses s-a-t with three ants. Print oracle_turns=4. Report counts of cases run, mismatches, skipped budget cases and actual command/toolchain; a green scaffold test does not mean this campaign ran.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/oracle.json
go test -run TestDifferential -count=1 ./...
go test -fuzz=FuzzTranscript -fuzztime=10s
Verification:
• Oracle s-a-t with n=3: 4 turns. Direct edge with n=3: 3 turns.
  • Two length-two branches and n=3: 3 turns. Unreachable end: no-route only after exhaustive search.
  • P07 greedy trap has V=8,n=4 and exceeds both the generic V≤6 and n≤3 oracle limits: add a separately budgeted targeted run with an explicit scope extension or a hand/exhaustive cut proof. Never silently run it under a stated n≤3 bound.
  • V=2..5,n=1..3 baseline: exactly 3294 graph/ant cases, including disconnected graphs. Count resource skips explicitly.
  • Corrupt one field per transcript: duplicate ant, nonedge, repeated undirected tunnel, room collision, early EOF, extra turn, invalid name and echo mismatch.
  • Fuzz parser inputs: bounded termination, no panic and no accepted partial model.

Exit gate

Provide a reproducible report with toolchain, seeds, case counts, discrepancies and skipped-budget counts. Distinguish tested examples from general proof; the oracle complements rather than replaces the P09/P10 correctness arguments.

Title: Deterministic and Bounded Release Lab
Summary: Build preflight budgets, deterministic output and a reproducible Go-only release checklist that preserves exactness under failure.
Overview:
Build the operational boundary around the planner: checked model-size estimates, a budget policy, stable transcript formatting and repeatable release evidence. The artifact is a small release harness plus tests proving that limits and output handling do not silently change the optimization problem.

Reuse the algorithms from P10 and the checker/oracle from P11. Your new work handles overflow, process streams, cancellation and repeatability. An honest refusal is preferable to labelling an unproved heuristic answer as a minimum-turn solution.
Refresher:
Signed integer overflow in Go does not panic automatically. Check multiplication and addition before creating time-layer counts, capacities, buffer lengths or slices. Perform calculations in a fixed-width type and verify conversion to int on the required 64-bit target.

For T layers of transitions, estimate 2(T+1)V+2TE vertices and at most (2T+1)V+5TE original arcs; residual arcs double the latter. Limits must be checked before allocation. Also bound accumulated output and work across all binary-search probes.

Keep three outcomes distinct: invalid input, a mathematically infeasible deadline, and inability to complete a computation within a resource budget. A timeout cannot be converted into false in binary search. A writer failure may happen after bytes have reached stdout; report it and exit without pretending the transcript is complete.

Logical turn concurrency does not require goroutines. A deterministic single-threaded planner is easier to bound and reproduce.
Spec:
1. Implement checked network-size estimation from V,E,T. Invalid negative parameters and arithmetic overflow are errors. Return int64 counts before any potentially unsafe conversion.
  2. Academy default limits: 1 MiB input, 4096-byte physical lines, 10000 ants, 10000 rooms, 50000 tunnels, 200000 expanded vertices, 1000000 stored residual arcs, 4000000 stored ant-time position cells, 16 MiB formatted output and a 240-second planning deadline. These are academy resource policies, not upstream graph-size guarantees.
  3. Check budgets before allocation and periodically during BFS augmentation, deadline probes and extraction. On exhaustion return a distinct error and no claimed optimal plan. Never substitute a greedy result. Allow a documented instructor-configured budget without weakening exactness.
  4. Format a complete accepted transcript only after parsing, planning and independent movement validation. Keep diagnostics off successful stdout. Canonical token order is ascending ant ID, single ASCII spaces, LF lines and no trailing spaces.
  5. For final L01: success exit 0; malformed/no-route input prints one ERROR: invalid data format line with optional suffix to stdout, exit 1; usage/I/O errors go to stderr, exit 2; resource exhaustion goes to stderr as ERROR: resource limit exceeded, exit 3. Writer failure is an I/O error; never print a second error into an already partial success transcript.
  6. The prep CLI prints vertices=36 original_arcs=51 residual_arcs=102 for V=3,E=2,T=3. Keep the final process adapter as a separate future component.
  7. Release evidence includes gofmt, tests, vet, a standard-library dependency inspection, 20 repeated-output comparisons, boundary resource tests and recorded performance hardware/toolchain. Upstream timing gates: example06 with 100 ants below 90 seconds, example07 with 1000 below 150 seconds; do not claim those measurements before running a finished solver.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go list -deps ./...
go run . testdata/budget.json
Verification:
For V=3,E=2,T=3, the upper counts are vertices=36 original_arcs=51 residual_arcs=102. Derive each count independently from the model.

  • V=2,E=1,T=1: 10 vertices, 11 original arcs, 22 residual arcs as an upper estimate; omitting end connector entries may reduce actual arcs.
  • Negative parameters and overflowing products: error before allocation.
  • Configured vertex budget 35 for the 36-vertex example: resource error, never infeasible.
  • Writer failure after a prefix: I/O exit and no appended invalid-data line.
  • Twenty identical runs produce exact byte equality.
  • Audit timing results remain pending until a completed solver is benchmarked on recorded hardware.

Exit gate

Explain every configured limit, its effect on valid but oversized input and why it cannot weaken the exactness claim for successful runs.

Title: Lem-in: Minimum-Turn Colony
Summary: Integrate the prepared Go components into a file-driven lem-in CLI with exact minimum-turn planning and independent movement validation.
Overview:
Build the actual lem-in executable. It accepts one colony file, finds a legal schedule delivering every ant in the fewest turns, echoes the accepted input and prints one movement line per turn. This is the integration assignment, not a new opportunity to replace exact planning with a greedy shortcut.

Reuse the reader from P02, grammar from P03, graph from P04, BFS from P05, independent checker from P06, residual engine from P08, time model from P09, exact planner from P10 and evidence tools from P11/P12. P01 supplies Go foundations; P07 explains allocation and greedy failure. Port these into one module with clear package boundaries and no third-party dependencies.

Deliverable

Source, meaningful tests, adversarial fixtures, a README with the published academy policies and algorithm proof, repeatable verification commands, a complexity/resource note and measured audit compatibility results. The supplied starter deliberately contains no solver.
Refresher:
The pipeline is read → parse → canonical graph → reachability → exact deadline search → trajectory extraction → independent replay → format → write. Each boundary has a typed result or error. Do not echo anything before the complete plan has passed validation.

For a graph with shortest distance d and n ants, search deadlines in [d,d+n-1]. Each deadline uses integral max flow on a time-expanded network with room splits, holdovers and one shared tunnel bottleneck per turn. Successful flow becomes n trajectories; omitted movements are waits. A BFS lower bound or exhausted T-1 cut supports the minimum-turn claim.

The upstream second usage example demonstrates pipelining into a room vacated that turn. The academy interprets turns as batches with departures before arrivals, validates occupancy at each boundary and sorts tokens by ant ID. Ant identity never grants extra room or tunnel capacity.

type Schedule struct { Turns [][]Move }
// These boundaries remain your implementation work:
// ReadColony, Optimize, ValidateSchedule, FormatTranscript, Execute.

Read the full academy policy and assignment brief. Local decisions are labelled; the original upstream snapshots are retained separately.
Spec:
Mandatory behavior

  1. Name the compiled CLI lem-in. Accept exactly one file argument. Read the colony from that file; stdin is not a substitute for the mandatory argument.
  2. Start n numbered ants at start and deliver all to end in the minimum number of movement turns. Each ant moves at most once per turn along one existing tunnel. Ordinary rooms hold at most one ant; start/end have unlimited occupancy. Each undirected tunnel is used once at most per turn.
  3. Accept room names, coordinates, commands and tunnels under the complete published grammar. Names are not assumed numeric or ordered. Coordinates are signed ints used only by the bonus. Ignore unknown commands semantically while retaining them in the accepted echo.
  4. Reject malformed counts, missing or duplicate terminals, duplicate rooms, invalid/overflowing coordinates, bad endpoint syntax, unknown endpoints, self-links, duplicate/reversed tunnels and no route. Ordinary cycles and disconnected extra rooms are valid if a start-end route remains.
  5. Use the exact P09/P10 method, or submit an alternative exact algorithm with a comparably complete correctness argument and independent evidence. A fixed greedy route set, maximum disjoint-path count alone, or one BFS path is insufficient.
  6. Success stdout is normalized accepted input with one final LF, one additional blank separator line, then nonempty movement lines. Tokens are L<ant>-<destination-name>, ascending ant ID within a turn, separated by one ASCII space and no trailing spaces. End the transcript with LF.
  7. Ant IDs are stable: canonicalize names/edges, use stable model arc insertion and unit extraction order, assign IDs 1..n by extraction. Multiple valid optima may differ between independently written solvers; repeated runs of one implementation must match exactly.
  8. Use the process stream and exit contract from P12. Invalid data/no route: stdout error prefix and exit 1, no echo. Usage/I/O: stderr and exit 2. Resource refusal: stderr and exit 3, no claimed plan. Success: exit 0.
  9. Keep assessed code standard-library-only. Include meaningful unit, integration, mutation and fuzz tests. Explain resource limits and all successful-run exactness guarantees. Publish performance evidence for the upstream audit examples before claiming audit readiness.

Academy additions and scope

The stricter numeric spelling, ambiguous hyphen resolution, whitespace/echo policy, simultaneous turn convention, ordering, streams, exits and budgets are academy policies. They are independently testable and may need adjustment if the local institution uses different interpretations. The GIF visualizer is a separate optional project after P13/P14. No GUI, browser JavaScript, third-party graph library or ready-made solver is required.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build -o lem-in .
# Windows executable name: go build -o lem-in.exe .
go run . testdata/corridor.txt
# Unix: ./lem-in testdata/corridor.txt
# Windows PowerShell: .\lem-in.exe testdata/corridor.txt
Verification:
One valid optimum, not an ID assignment oracle

For the supplied three-ant corridor, a valid four-turn suffix is:

L1-a
L1-t L2-a
L2-t L3-a
L3-t

Your deterministic extraction may assign IDs differently. The checker must still find four legal turns, all ants at end and valid output spelling. Compare exact bytes only across repeated runs of your own declared tie-breaking implementation.

Required evidence cases

  • Direct edge, n=3: three turns; two disjoint length-two branches, n=3: three turns.
  • P07 greedy trap, n=4: minimum five turns; a six-turn shortest-only answer fails optimality.
  • Ordinary cycle, disconnected extra room and nonnumeric unordered names: accepted when a route exists.
  • Every P03 grammar mutation and every P06 movement mutation: deliberately classified.
  • P11's 3294 tiny graph/ant cases: compare optimum and replay every returned plan; report all skips.
  • Source examples 00..05: audit ceilings 6,8,11,6,6,8 respectively. Treat ceilings as compatibility checks, not proof that every displayed upstream schedule is optimal.
  • Source examples 06/07 with 100/1000 ants: below 90/150 seconds on recorded hardware for audit readiness.
  • Same input 20 runs: identical output. Limits, cancellation and failing writers: no crash or false optimality claim.

Final exit gate

Source builds, tests and vet pass; acceptance tests are enabled; no TODO core stubs remain; dependency review is standard-library-only; every returned schedule is legal; exactness proof and independent tiny evidence agree; process and resource behavior are documented. Instructor review is required before claiming readiness. This hub does not mark learner completion.

Title: Replay Stream Decoder
Summary: Build a bounded stdin replay decoder that validates a lem-in transcript and exposes immutable room snapshots for rendering.
Overview:
Build a streaming replay inspection tool for completed lem-in output. It separates echoed colony data from movements, validates the replay and emits a text table of ant positions at turn boundaries. This is the data foundation for the optional visualizer; it does not create images yet.

Reuse P11's transcript grammar and P06's independent movement rules after L01 is ready. The new work is a Reader-based consumer, immutable snapshots, stdin EOF, producer failure and text/binary stream boundaries. The renderer in P14 should never have to parse movement tokens itself.
Refresher:
A producer's stdout becomes the consumer's stdin. EOF only means the stream ended; it does not prove all ants arrived. A solver invalid-data line is not a valid replay. The decoder must reject it rather than create an empty animation.

A snapshot is the full position array at one boundary, including turn 0. Copy each slice when storing history. Appending the same mutable slice repeatedly produces frames that all show the final state.

type Snapshot struct {
    Turn int
    Positions []int // caller-visible immutable copy
}

Consume the declared echo, one blank separator and movement batches. Support hyphenated destination names by splitting the ant prefix only once. Validate each turn before exposing its next snapshot. Rendering may interpolate between snapshots, but must not invent different logical motion.
Spec:
1. Implement Decode(r,maxBytes) for the academy transcript grammar. Apply a 16 MiB stream cap, line cap and bounded ant/turn counts, and at most 4000000 stored ant-time position cells. Check history growth before copying a next snapshot. Unknown commands remain in the echoed colony but have no movement meaning.
  2. Return colony room names/coordinates, tunnels, start/end, and immutable snapshots for boundaries 0..T. Validate all tokens and turns independently, require every ant at end and forbid extra movement after completion.
  3. Reject malformed echo, missing/extra separator, truncated replay, invalid-data solver output, bad ant IDs, unknown destinations, room/tunnel violations and Reader failures. Return no accepted replay on error.
  4. Snapshot 0 contains every ant at start. Waiting ants retain positions. Arrived ants stay at end. Store stable room indices from the canonical graph and preserve a room-name legend.
  5. The CLI accepts zero arguments for stdin or one transcript path for fixtures. Print a text table with turn=K positions=name,... in ant ID order.
  6. Include an integration test using Go os/exec or io.Pipe that handles producer errors and closes pipes. Do not equate pipeline EOF with producer success.
  7. PowerShell versions differ in native pipeline byte handling. For exact UTF-8 cross-process tests, use a small Go os/exec harness connecting streams directly; the simple native pipe remains the published usage example. No student JavaScript or external package is required.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/transcript.txt
# After building: ./lem-in colony.txt | ./replay-decoder
# Windows native command prefix: .\
Verification:
The fixture's snapshots must be:

turn=0 positions=s,s
turn=1 positions=a,s
turn=2 positions=t,a
turn=3 positions=t,t
  • Delete the final movement: incomplete replay error.
  • Append a movement after completion: rejected.
  • Use L1-west-hall for an existing hyphenated room: decode the full destination.
  • Keep one ant stationary during a turn: its position is retained.
  • Mutate one returned snapshot in a test and verify others do not share storage.
  • Send a Reader error after a valid prefix: no accepted replay.

Exit gate

The decoder exposes only fully validated histories and does not import planner logic. Demonstrate a portable Go pipeline test and describe the shell byte-handling assumption separately.

Title: Go Raster and GIF Studio
Summary: Build a deterministic coordinate mapper, line/disc renderer and bounded animated GIF encoder using only Go's standard library.
Overview:
Build an image studio that draws a tiny colony scene and animates a supplied dot trajectory into a GIF. It is independent from lem-in parsing so you can learn coordinate transforms, raster primitives, palettes and frame timing without debugging a stream decoder at the same time.

Reuse P13's concept of immutable boundary snapshots. The new artifact is a Go renderer with PNG keyframes for inspection, an animated GIF and a text legend. Go has standard image encoders but no standard GUI toolkit or font rasterizer; a small numeric bitmap glyph set or an external text legend keeps the bonus feasible without extra packages.
Refresher:
Model coordinates may be negative, coincident or very large. Convert each coordinate to float64 before subtracting to avoid signed integer overflow. Fit the bounding box into the viewport with padding and one uniform scale so distances keep their aspect ratio. If an axis span is zero, center it rather than dividing by zero. Invert y if your display policy treats upward model coordinates as upward on screen.

A paletted frame stores one color index per pixel. Use a fixed palette with a dark background, pale tunnels, distinct rooms and high-contrast ants. Check bounds before setting pixels. Full independent frames are simpler than delta frames; choose a disposal policy deliberately so trails do not accumulate.

GIF delay units are hundredths of a second. If each logical turn has four interpolation frames and lasts 0.4 seconds, each frame delay is 10. Keep the initial and final state visible. EncodeAll stores frames in memory, so total pixels across frames need their own budget.

type Pixel struct { X, Y int }
type FrameSpec struct { Positions []Pixel; Delay int }
// The mapping, drawing and frame sequencing are your core work.
Spec:
1. Implement a deterministic fit transform into a default 320×240 image with 20-pixel padding. Accept signed coordinates, preserve aspect ratio, center zero-span axes and reject invalid dimensions or nonfinite derived values.
  2. Draw tunnels as clipped or bounds-checked line segments, rooms as fixed-radius discs and ant positions as distinct high-contrast discs. Draw in stable edge, room and ant order.
  3. Use only image, image/color, image/draw, image/png, image/gif and other standard packages. Do not add golang.org/x/image/font, GUI libraries or browser JavaScript.
  4. Room names may be arbitrary valid grammar names. Write a UTF-8 text legend mapping stable room IDs to names and coordinates. Numeric glyphs are an optional hand-built bitmap feature, not a third-party font requirement.
  5. Require at least two boundary snapshots with the same positive number of positions and valid image coordinates. Render full independent paletted frames. Add four interpolation frames between supplied turn boundaries, using linear interpolation for moving ants and fixed positions for waiting ants. The final keyframe must match the next boundary exactly.
  6. Default per-turn time is 40 hundredths of a second; distribute it into four equal delays. Add initial/final holds of 40 units. Specify GIF LoopCount=0 and a disposal strategy that avoids trails.
  7. Maximum dimensions 1280×720, at most 2000 frames and 50000000 total stored pixels. Preflight checked width×height×frameCount; report a resource error before allocating beyond the budget. Never silently crop frames or omit turns.
  8. The CLI reads the supplied JSON dot sequence and writes studio.gif, first.png, last.png and legend.txt in the current directory only after validating the request. Fail cleanly on output errors.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run . testdata/studio.json
Verification:
• Two snapshots with one moving dot produce six frames with delays [40,10,10,10,10,40].
  • All coordinates equal: centered scene without divide-by-zero.
  • Negative and near-int64-extreme coordinates: no integer overflow or nonfinite transform.
  • A line ending at an image boundary and a disc crossing padding: no out-of-bounds panic.
  • Decode the GIF back: dimensions, frame count, palette and delays are as declared.
  • Mutate one frame after rendering and verify another frame's pixels do not change.
  • Budget one pixel below the required total: resource error before frame allocation.

Exit gate

Inspect the first/last PNG and GIF in a viewer, verify no trails or missing endpoint frames and keep a text legend. Pixel/metadata tests and visual inspection serve different purposes.

Title: Optional Ant-Farm GIF Visualizer
Summary: Combine the Go replay decoder and raster studio into a pipeline consumer that writes an animated colony GIF and a text replay.
Overview:
Build visualizer, a Go-only consumer of valid lem-in stdout. It reads the echoed colony and ant movements from stdin, validates them, then writes an animated GIF showing ants travelling through the coordinate-defined colony. It also writes a legend and a text replay so the data remains reviewable without animation.

Reuse P13's immutable validated history and P14's mapper, raster primitives and GIF encoder. Core lem-in must already pass its own readiness gates. The bonus visualizes a schedule; it does not make a slow schedule optimal or repair an illegal one.

Feasible standard-library scope

GIF is the chosen rendering target because Go's standard library provides raster images and GIF encoding. An installed image viewer or browser can display the file without student JavaScript, a GUI toolkit or a third-party graphics package. A 3D visualizer is mentioned as an extra in the upstream audit, but is not required by this academy's optional 2D bonus.
Refresher:
Composition should keep parsing, simulation and rendering independent. P13 produces a validated history with room names, coordinates, tunnels and one position per ant at each boundary. P14 maps the fixed scene once and draws frames from those positions.

Interpolate only movement positions between validated boundaries. An ant traverses the drawn tunnel from its old room to its new one; waiting ants stay fixed. Collocated start/end ants can be rendered as a deterministic compact cluster or an aggregate marker, while the companion text preserves every ID.

Preflight the whole output before large frame allocation. A GIF is binary output, so do not mix diagnostic text into it. This academy writes binary GIF to a named file and leaves stdout available for a concise file summary. Invalid input must not leave an apparently successful final GIF.

// Published interface after students finish both executables:
// ./lem-in ant-farm.txt | ./visualizer
// Result: farm.gif, legend.txt, replay.txt in the current directory.
Spec:
1. Compile the CLI as visualizer. With no arguments read stdin and write farm.gif, legend.txt and replay.txt. Optionally support -out path.gif, with companion files in the same selected directory.
  2. Decode the complete academy transcript using P13, independently validate legal movement and completion, and reject solver error output, malformed/truncated streams and Reader failures. A legal but suboptimal transcript can be visualized; label the output as a replay, never a proof of optimum.
  3. Draw every room and tunnel from the colony. Fit the supplied coordinates with P14's aspect-preserving transform, including negatives, zero spans and coincidences. Room identity is independent from coordinates.
  4. Use four interpolation frames per logical turn at the declared timing, plus initial/final holds. Draw ants moving along their actual tunnels; keep waiting/arrived ants represented. End on the actual all-end snapshot.
  5. Preserve names and every ant's identity in legend/replay text. If the image aggregates terminal ants or separates coincident markers for visibility, document that display policy and retain exact positions in the companion text.
  6. Keep all student code standard-library-only, with no browser script, third-party fonts, graphics library or external encoder. GIF, PNG and text files are generated by Go.
  7. Apply P13's input bounds and P14's frame, dimension and total-pixel bounds; check arithmetic before allocation. Return a distinct resource error without dropping turns, shrinking the requested dimensions silently or presenting a partial final GIF as success.
  8. Use temporary files in the destination directory while writing. Finalize only after encoding and closing succeed; clean up owned temporary files on failure. Do not overwrite an existing output set without an explicit documented -overwrite flag. Multi-file rename is not fully atomic: document cleanup and rollback behavior.
  9. On success stdout names the three files; diagnostics go to stderr and failures return nonzero. No auto-opening viewer is required. Include decode-back metadata tests, logical-boundary pixel checks, pipeline tests and actual visual inspection.
Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build -o visualizer .
# Windows executable name: go build -o visualizer.exe .
# Unix, after building the completed solver:
# ./lem-in colony.txt | ./visualizer
# Windows PowerShell native pipeline:
# .\lem-in.exe colony.txt | .\visualizer.exe
# For byte-exact portable tests, connect processes with Go os/exec.
# POSIX shell fixture: go run . < testdata/transcript.txt
# PowerShell: use the Go os/exec test harness for exact input bytes.
Verification:
The fixture contains three turns, so expect 14 GIF frames at the configured four-subframe rate, with first/last holds of 40 centiseconds. All ants must end at t in replay.txt.

  • Corridor, two-branch colony, negative coordinates, zero-span axes and coincident rooms: all render without panic.
  • Hyphenated and UTF-8 names survive the legend; names need not fit inside a room marker.
  • Decode the output with gif.DecodeAll and compare frame dimensions, count, delays and final keyframe pixels.
  • Invalid solver output, truncated replay, bad move and resource breach: no final success artifact.
  • Existing output files without -overwrite: clear error and unchanged files.
  • Inspect real motion in a viewer; compare several logical boundaries with replay.txt, checking waits, terminal crowds and no trails.

Exit gate

Core L01 readiness remains separate. The optional bonus is review-ready only after a real pipeline, decode-back checks, failure cleanup tests and viewed animation pass. Record any untested shell/viewer combinations honestly.
